lesson.title: Why the Second Lookup Is Free: DNS Caching and TTLs
lesson.summary: DNS answers are cached at several layers between a client and the authoritative server, each governed by a time to live value, so most lookups skip the full root to TLD to authoritative walk entirely.
lesson.body:
Walking the full chain from a root server through a TLD server to an authoritative server, as the recursive resolver chapter traced for www.example.com, works, but doing it for every single request from every single client would be slow and would put enormous load on a small number of root and TLD servers. DNS avoids almost all of that repeated work through caching, remembering an answer for a while instead of asking again.

Every DNS record carries a time to live, or TTL, a number of seconds set by the authoritative server that owns the record. The TTL tells everyone downstream exactly how long they are allowed to reuse that answer before they have to ask again. If the A record for www.example.com has a TTL of 3600, any resolver that learns 192.0.2.10 from ns1.example.com can keep answering that question itself for a full hour, for any client that asks, without contacting the authoritative server again.

Caching happens at more than one layer, and each layer shortens the walk a little more. A browser may keep its own short lived cache of recent lookups. The operating system's stub resolver often keeps one too. The big one, though, is the recursive resolver's cache, since it is shared across every client that uses that resolver, an ISP's entire customer base or everyone using a given public resolver. Once that resolver has learned the referral to the com TLD servers, or the referral to example.com's authoritative servers, or the final A record itself, it can reuse each of those cached pieces independently for as long as their individual TTLs allow, which is exactly why the root and TLD steps of the trace so often get skipped on the second lookup and every lookup after it.

TTL length is a genuine trade off, not just a technical detail. A long TTL, hours or a day, means fewer repeated lookups, faster responses for users, and less load on the authoritative infrastructure, but it also means that if the domain owner changes the record, for instance moving example.com to a new server, cached copies around the world keep sending traffic to the old address until their TTLs expire. That is exactly why administrators planning a migration will often lower a record's TTL to something short, like 300 seconds, well ahead of time, so that once the real change happens it propagates quickly instead of being stuck behind hours of stale cached answers.

You can see the effect of caching directly in ordinary DNS tools: a fresh answer straight from the authoritative server comes back marked authoritative, exactly as described in the previous chapter, while a resolver serving the same answer from its cache a minute later marks it non authoritative, the same data, reused rather than re fetched.
